statement: In triangle $ABC$, $AB = 7$, $AC = 8$ and $\angle BAC = 60^\circ$. What is the radius of the circle that passes through $A$, $B$ and $C$?

choices.misconception: I found BC = sqrt(57) and then took the circumradius to be half of BC, as if BC were a diameter, which only happens when the angle at A is a right angle.
I used the law of cosines with a plus sign, getting BC^2 = 49 + 64 + 56 = 169 and BC = 13, then divided 13 by 2 sin 60 degrees.
I set up R = BC / (2 sin A) correctly but used sin 60 degrees = 1/2, so the denominator became 1 and R came out equal to BC.
I used BC / sin A = R, forgetting that the extended law of sines says BC / sin A equals the diameter 2R, not the radius.

hints: First find the side opposite the $60^\circ$ angle.
The law of cosines gives $BC$. Then the extended law of sines links one side, its opposite angle and the circumradius.

solutions.reliable: By the law of cosines, $BC^2 = 7^2 + 8^2 - 2\cdot 7\cdot 8\cos 60^\circ = 49 + 64 - 56 = 57$, so $BC = \sqrt{57}$. The extended law of sines gives $2R = \dfrac{BC}{\sin A} = \dfrac{\sqrt{57}}{\sqrt3/2}$, so $R = \dfrac{\sqrt{57}}{\sqrt3} = \sqrt{19}$. Check with $R = \dfrac{abc}{4K}$: $K = \tfrac12\cdot 7\cdot 8\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} = 14\sqrt3$, and $\dfrac{7\cdot 8\cdot\sqrt{57}}{56\sqrt3} = \sqrt{19}$. The idea: one side plus its opposite angle fixes the circumradius.
solutions.elegant: Draw the diameter $BX$ of the circumcircle. The inscribed angle $\angle BXC$ equals $\angle BAC = 60^\circ$ and $\angle BCX = 90^\circ$, so $BC = 2R\sin 60^\circ = R\sqrt3$. With $BC = \sqrt{57}$ this gives $R = \sqrt{19}$.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
